html:
Cape Town is the oldest city in South Africa, beneath Table Mountain near the Cape of Good Hope, and the seat of the country's parliament. It began in 1652 as a supply station of the Dutch East India Company, where ships sailing between Europe and Asia took on fresh water, meat and vegetables.

The land belonged to Khoekhoe herders, who lost their pastures as the station grew into the Cape Colony and its farmers spread inland as the Dutch settlements at the Cape. The company brought enslaved people from Madagascar, India and the East Indies; their descendants include the Cape Malay community, and its language mixed into what became Afrikaans.

Britain took the Cape in 1795 and for good in 1806, and Cape Town became the capital of a British colony and a port of empire. The University of Cape Town grew from a college founded in 1829. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, Cape Town became the seat of parliament.

Under apartheid the government drove tens of thousands of people of colour out of the mixed inner-city area in the District Six removals, and held Nelson Mandela on Robben Island in the bay for eighteen years. In 1967 a surgical team at Groote Schuur Hospital performed the first human heart transplant. Mandela gave his first speech after his release from the city hall balcony in 1990.
